memoryText: For I know the plans I have for you, declares the LORD, plans for welfare and not for evil, to give you a future and a hope.
readingInstruction: No new reading today. Read Jeremiah 29:11 slowly, several times, and then say it from memory. Read the meditation and the week in review, and choose one of the three questions to write about, pray over, or share with someone.
memoryVerseMeditation:
This is one of the most quoted verses in the Bible, and it is often quoted out of context. To hear it as Jeremiah’s first readers did, remember who it was written to.

It was written to exiles, people who had lost their city, their temple, and their king. They were in a foreign land with no sign of returning. False prophets were telling them it would be over soon. Then Jeremiah’s letter arrived, and it said that they would be there for seventy years. After that, this promise: “For I know the plans I have for you.”

The first thing it says is that God has plans. The exile was not an accident. It was part of what he was doing. The second is that he knows them. We often do not know the plans, and we do not need to, because he knows them. The third is that they are “plans for welfare,” shalom, wholeness, “and not for evil.” The word for evil is the word for calamity. The exile looked like calamity, but God’s purpose was good.

Finally, “to give you a future and a hope.” The future is real. The hope is not a wish but an expectation based on God’s word. In the same chapter, God says he will bring them back. The promise does not remove the seventy years. It gives them meaning.

This verse does not promise an easy life. It promises that the one who holds your future is good. For Christians, the ultimate fulfillment is in Christ, in whom all of God’s promises are “Yes.” Say this verse when you do not know what comes next.
weekInReview: This week you followed Jeremiah through the rest of his early ministry. You read the king’s last warnings and the promise of a righteous Branch whose name is “The LORD is our righteousness.” You saw the vision of two baskets of figs, in which the exiles were the good figs. You read about the cup of wrath, the seventy years, the yoke of Babylon, and the false prophet Hananiah. Then you read the letter to the exiles, which told them to build, plant, and seek the welfare of the city. You prayed Psalms 102 and 103, the cry of the afflicted and the praise of the God who removes our sins as far as the east is from the west, and Psalm 106, a history of rebellion and mercy. The week taught that God is sovereign over exile, that false hope is dangerous, and that his plans for his people are for welfare and a future.
reflectionQuestions: Jeremiah told the exiles to seek the welfare of Babylon. How can you seek the good of the place where God has put you this week?
Psalm 103 says God removes our transgressions as far as the east is from the west. Where do you still carry guilt that Christ has already carried?
The false prophets promised quick relief, and Jeremiah promised a long road with a sure hope. Which do you tend to want, and how does Jeremiah 29:11 speak to that?
prayerPrompts: Thank God for his plans for your welfare and a future and a hope.
Ask him to teach you to seek the good of the place he has put you.
Rest in his faithfulness this Sabbath.
